With your powers combined…

This colorful picture of the cosmos is the product of teamwork between our @NASAHubble, @NASAWebb, and @NASAChandraXray telescopes. Scientists brought their data together to get a vibrant look at this star-forming region known as the Tarantula Nebula, located 160,000 light-years from Earth.

Chandra’s X-ray data fills in the deep blue parts of the image, showing the gas blown away by the stellar winds created by the nebula’s young stars. Webb’s infrared data shows up as red, displaying the thousands of stars and the dust that gives rise to them. Hubble’s visible dat

Soothing spacewalk scenes. 

Today, August 18, NASA’s @astro_anil and ESA’s @soph_astro completed a 6 hour, 23 minute spacewalk to remove a failed communications antenna and stow it outside the International Space Station. These challenging tasks are accompanied by rewarding views as the orbiting laboratory continues soaring at 17,500 miles per hour over our blue marble below. The next spacewalk is scheduled for Tuesday, August 25.

When the Moon and Sun align

This rare sight — a total solar eclipse — was photographed in San Millán de los Caballeros, Spain, on Aug. 12.

The Sun is 400 times wider than the Moon, but in a cosmic coincidence, it's also 400 times further away. This means that they appear to be the same size in our sky — and when the Moon passes in front, it can perfectly block the Sun.

Credit: NASA

#NASA #Eclipse #TotalSolarEclipse

Cementing their names in history.

The Artemis III crew is leaving their mark — literally. The astronauts recently signed their names on the hardware that will be inside their Orion spacecraft during their low Earth orbit mission, launching in 2027.

Some things are worth repeating 📸

Like observing a galaxy cluster! This image of the cluster Abell S0740 was created by combining several @NASAHubble science observations. Hubble's multiple looks at the cluster revealed a diverse collection of galaxies including a giant, bright elliptical galaxy just off center. That galaxy is as massive as 100 billion of our Suns, by the way.
 
Credit: NASA

#NASA #Hubble #Stars

Curly-haired crew, this one’s for you! 🌀🚀👩🏻‍🦱

Join me in my temporary home on the @iss, where curls are even more free to be what they want to be. Ever wonder how I care for my curls in space?…where my Earthly 3a curls become more like 3c, my hair finds every piece of velcro it can, and I STILL don’t need a brush! 

There are definitely some major pros to my space hair, like not having to put it up when I work out. 💪

I’m looking forward to an Earth shower when I get back, though. 🚿🌎

Hey, neighbor

Did you know our home galaxy — the Milky Way — has smaller galaxies that orbit around it? The biggest one, called the Large Magellanic Cloud, is "only" 160,000 light-years away. It's known for giving astronomers great views of newly-forming stars, like in the nebula seen here.

The bubble in this image, as shown by @NASAHubble, was created by the stars in the center pushing out the gas around them when they were born. Now, other stars are forming in this compressed gas shell — starting the cycle anew.

Credit: NASA

It is currently on its way to its destination 1 million miles from Earth, where it will change how we view the cosmos and help us to unravel some of the greatest mysteries of the universe.

You may have seen this spacewalk titled "U.S. Spacewalk 99," but what does that really mean? While this was the 284th spacewalk ever performed on the space station, it was only the 99th done in NASA spacesuits out of the station’s Quest airlock.

Red Moon over Louisiana

On the night of Aug. 27-28, the full moon slipped through Earth's shadow, creating a near-total lunar eclipse for skywatchers in the Americas. (Viewers in Europe and Africa were able to catch a partial lunar eclipse, as well.) 

Because the remaining light is largely filtered through Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter frequencies like violets and blues, the light that reaches the Moon can take on a reddish tone.

Space swabs for science! 🦠

Astronauts @soph_astro and @astro_jessica stepped outside of the space station last week. During their spacewalk, @soph_astro collected samples near life support systems as part of a study to track if microbes are released from the space station and how they may survive.

Samples from an earlier spacewalk found that the airlock contained the most microbial DNA. New samples could reveal how microbes may spread from a spacecraft and help scientists limit contamination on future missions to the Moon and beyond.

It is thought that the irregular appearance of Arp 263 is actually due to a galactic merger. Galactic mergers cause gas and dust to crash together, and that process creates stars.

In some galaxies, such as many elliptical galaxies, there is little star formation taking place. Other galaxies, like our Milky Way, have a moderate amount of newborn stars. Still others, called starburst galaxies, are experiencing a sudden and short-lived period of rampant stellar birth.

Galactic Gems Galore!🌀

Galaxies are cosmic gems — each with characteristics including size and shape that make them distinct.

Just as gems reveal the history of the Earth through how they were forged over billions of years, these galactic gems are a way to study our Earth’s place in our home galaxy of the Milky Way. By looking outward to other galaxies, we learn more about our own — including clues to its past and future.

NASA telescopes weave a new view of the Tarantula Nebula 🕷️

Located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small neighbor galaxy to the Milky Way about 160,000 light-years from Earth, the Tarantula Nebula has thousands of young stars embedded in a radiant honeycomb-like structure of gas and dust.

Like a collage made of layered sheets of colored cellophane, this new image layers views of the Tarantula Nebula made in different types of light by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory (X-ray light), Hubble Space Telescope (optical light), and Webb Space Telescope (infrared light).

Here Webb captures a different aspect of Carina: a feature called the Treasure Chest, which is an object known as a cometary globule.

Webb's look at the Lion Nebula, actually the remains of a dying lower-mass star, is in both the mid and near-infrared. Though massive stars undergo supernova explosions at the end of their lives, lower-mass stars like this one shed their outer layers, which turn into the shells of dust and gas you see here. At the center remains the hot stellar core, known as a white dwarf.

Who doesn't love a good mystery?! 🔍🔴

Little Red Dots (LRD), have puzzled astronomers ever since Webb first detected them in 2022. They are compact objects that are very distant, seemed to emerge in large numbers about 600 million years after the big bang, and then mysteriously decline by about 1.5 billion years post-big bang. Are they a new class of galaxy? Or some sort of active supermassive black hole? Where did they go as the universe matured?

What if they didn’t actually disappear, they just look different when they are less distant?
